name: Benin
summary: Independent from France as Dahomey in 1960; renamed Benin in 1975. Its 1990 national conference was one of Africa’s first peaceful moves to democracy.

knownFor.label: Vodun
knownFor.note: Benin is the birthplace of Vodun (voodoo).

location.value: West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; about 113,000–115,000 km² (sources give 114,763 km² and 112,622 km²).

terrain.value: A narrow strip from the Atlantic coast, with lagoons, the low Allada plateau, and hills and savanna in the north.

climate.value: Tropical, with two rainy seasons in the south and one in the north.

resources.value: Cotton (the main export), palm oil, cashews and shea nuts.

disasters.value: Floods along the Ouémé River and droughts in the north.

population.value: About 15.2 million (2026 estimate); about 13 million in 2021.

disease.value: Malaria is the main disease, with Lassa fever and cholera outbreaks at times.

migration.value: Heavy cross-border trade and movement with Nigeria, and many Beninese work abroad.

economicBase.value: Cotton and palm oil are the main exports; regional trade and transit are important.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country, with much of the economy informal.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

keyRulers.value: Mathieu Kérékou. Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Multi-party elections since 1991; observers called the 2026 vote not free or fair.

institutions.value: A National Assembly and a Constitutional Court, created under the 1990 constitution.

stability.value: Coups after independence; Marxist rule after Kérékou's 1972 coup, until about 1990.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small army, air force and navy, with participation in regional operations.

majorWars.value: No wars with other states; the country saw several coups in the 1960s–70s.

territoryChange.value: The borders drawn by France have remained the same since independence.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of ECOWAS and the West African Economic and Monetary Union; close to France and Nigeria.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Universities in Abomey-Calavi and Parakou; primary schooling has expanded.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The port of Cotonou and roads to the north carry goods, much of it headed to landlocked Niger.

religion.value: Christianity (53%), Islam (31%) and traditional or other faiths (11%).

languageWriting.value: French is official; Fon, Yoruba and many other languages are spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: The royal palaces of Abomey, a World Heritage Site, have bas-relief panels telling the Dahomey kings’ history.

socialStructure.value: Fon, Yoruba, Bariba and many other ethnic groups.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in the heritage of the Dahomey kingdom and in the peaceful 1990 transition to democracy.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat maize or yam dishes, and the south is also home to Vodun traditions and festivals.

neighbours.value: Togo, Burkina Faso, Niger and Nigeria.

ideasReligions.value: Vodun spread to the Americas with enslaved people.

colonisation.value: A French colony until independence on 1 August 1960.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Benin continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
